problem: End-to-end VLN models generalize poorly to novel environments and complex instructions, while prior modular LLM/VLM approaches (VLMaps, CLIP-Nav, LM-Nav, Lang2LTL) handle only simple instructions or ground landmarks poorly (CLIP on semantic occupancy maps).
motivation: Zero-shot LLMs and VLMs offer strong language parsing and visual grounding without costly RL/IL training. The authors observe that grounding landmarks in per-node panoramas of a topological map with a stronger VLM (SigLIP) works far better than projecting CLIP embeddings into an occupancy map, and that path-instruction alignment can be scored interpretably via landmark grounding.
key_idea: Extract ordered landmarks with an LLM, retrieve top-k last-landmark nodes with SigLIP on a topological panorama map, generate shortest-path hypotheses, and rank them by a DP (LCS-like) alignment of GPT-4o landmark-grounding scores.
insight: Explicit decomposition into landmark grounding plus DP alignment (Approach I: 57.45 accuracy, 88.92 nDTW) beats prompting GPT-4o to rate whole paths with the full instruction (Approach II: 50.15, 88.34), suggesting VLMs struggle to ground actions and landmarks jointly. Panorama-based retrieval with SigLIP gives 70.0 Precision@10 vs 34.4 for VLMaps with CLIP. Path-hypothesis generation accuracy (65.72) caps the final performance, so last-landmark retrieval is the bottleneck.
method: Topological map: nodes are 360° RGB panoramas at all unique waypoints from R2R train episodes, edges have weight 1 for connectivity.
Landmark extraction: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (zero-shot) extracts the ordered landmark sequence from the instruction.
Goal retrieval: SigLIP cosine similarity between the last landmark text and node panoramas gives the top-k (k=3) goal nodes.
Path hypotheses: BFS shortest paths from the start node to each of the k goals; paths with fewer nodes than landmarks are discarded.
Approach I (Pano2Land): GPT-4o gives binary landmark-in-panorama grounding matrix; an LCS-style DP computes the normalized alignment score (matched landmarks / path length); the top path is selected.
Approach II: GPT-4o rates each path 1-5 given panorama sequence, instruction and landmarks (no explicit grounding).
Evaluation: nDTW between the selected path and ground truth; nDTW above 87% is counted as success; ties broken randomly over 3 repeats, reporting mean±std.

setting.backbone: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (frozen) for landmark extraction, SigLIP (frozen) for retrieval, GPT-4o (frozen) for grounding/ranking
setting.training_data: none (training-free); topological map built from R2R train episodes' waypoints
setting.observation: 360° RGB panoramas at topological map nodes
setting.action_space: discrete topological graph nodes (BFS shortest paths)
setting.privileged: Pre-built topological map of the test environment from R2R train-split waypoints (pre-exploration); each GT waypoint has a corresponding map node

numbers.eval_set_note: 5 environments x 21 episodes = 105 episodes (split not explicitly stated in the paper; val-unseen assumed)
numbers.extra: Known topological map built from train-split waypoints; success defined as nDTW>87%; top-3 goal hypotheses; mean of 3 random tie-breaks

numbers_note: The paper does not state which R2R split the 105 episodes come from; it only reports per-environment results on 5 scenes. 'Accuracy' is nDTW>87% success, not standard SR. No comparison with standard VLN baselines. The landmark retrieval result (Precision@10 70.0 vs VLMaps 34.4 on 127 landmarks) is not a navigation benchmark.
results: On 105 R2R-Habitat episodes across 5 environments, Approach I reaches 88.92 nDTW and 57.45% accuracy, better than GPT-4o full-sequence ranking (88.34 / 50.15). Last-landmark retrieval with SigLIP on panoramas achieves 70.0 Precision@10 versus 34.4 for VLMaps with CLIP.
limitations: Only works in previously explored environments with a pre-built topological map (no exploration or unseen-environment navigation).
Works only for landmark-centric instructions; action, spatial, temporal, and metric phrases are not handled.
Modular error propagation: the quality of landmark extraction and retrieval bounds ranking (hypothesis accuracy only 65.72%); evaluation is small (105 episodes) with a nonstandard success criterion.
